scenes.tts: "Please call me Max" were the first words Perutz offered almost every young scientist who came to him. He had a model of hemoglobin hanging from his office ceiling and had been chasing the one molecule since 1937 — twenty-two years before he solved it.

scenes.tts: The breakthrough was a trick: soak the crystals in mercury and silver to triangulate the missing information. Kendrew ran it first, on myoglobin.

scenes.tts: There was no computer screen in 1958, so the group drew the electron density by hand and stacked the contours on dozens of sheets of clear plastic until the molecule climbed up into three dimensions.
scenes.narration: There was no computer screen in 1958, so the group drew the electron density by hand and stacked the contours on dozens of sheets of clear plastic until the molecule climbed up into three dimensions.

scenes.tts: What rose out of the sheets was a fat, irregular rod doubling back on itself with no symmetry anyone had predicted — the lab called it the sausage model, and Kendrew admitted only to surprise at its "unexpected twists," conceding the shape could not be recommended on aesthetic grounds.

scenes.tts: The first protein ever seen was a mess. It was also exactly right. The two men shared the 1962 Nobel Prize.
